# The Last Light of Station Zero

The lighthouse was not on any map.

It stood on a jagged outcropping of black basalt, three miles offshore from the coast of Nova Scotia, in a stretch of water so deep and dark that the bottom was a rumor, a place where the ocean forgot how to end. The structure itself was a monstrosity of iron and glass, blackened by decades of salt spray and the relentless, howling wind. It was not built to save ships from the rocks, for there were no ships that came this way. It was not built to warn of storms, for the storms were the only things that ever visited.

Station #0 was a lighthouse built in the void, a beacon for nothing. And its keeper was Elias Thorne.

Elias had been the keeper for forty years.

He was a man carved from the same stone as the tower, weathered and stoic, with a beard the color of rust and eyes that had long since lost the ability to blink in surprise. His body was a map of the lighthouse’s history: a scar across his knuckles from a shattered lens in 1984, a limp in his left leg from a fall on the spiral stairs in 1999, and a permanent stiffness in his neck from years of looking up.

Every night, at exactly 11:58 PM, Elias would begin the ritual.

First, he would climb the 167 steps. The iron treads were slick with condensation, and the walls were damp, weeping cold air that smelled of brine and ancient dust. He moved slowly, his hand trailing along the railing, counting the steps in his head. *One, two, three… one hundred and
